extracted.intended_audience: researchers, clinicians, and guideline developers who conduct or use systematic reviews and meta-analyses
extracted.subtask_description: Background and rationale for the PRISMA reporting guideline, describing the problems in reporting of systematic reviews/meta-analyses, prior guidance (QUOROM), the original PRISMA, and the 2020 update process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value depends on methods, findings, and clarity of reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: As with all research, the value of a systematic review depends on what was done, what was found, and the clarity of reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This frames reporting as fundamental to the usefulness of a review: clear description of methods and findings is necessary for readers to interpret and apply results. Poor reporting reduces the review's value irrespective of the underlying work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting should enable assessment of strengths and weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers must be able to assess the strengths and weaknesses of systematic reviews; variation in reporting quality limits this ability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The historical studies cited found wide variation and generally poor reporting across many characteristics, which impeded readers' ability to judge review quality. Thus, a key reporting goal is transparency that allows appraisal of bias, applicability, and limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a quality assessment of included studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit reporting criteria should include reporting a quality assessment of included studies (example from early evaluations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early evaluations (e.g., Mulrow 1987) used items such as whether reviews reported assessment of the quality of included studies; omission of such assessments was a common deficiency. Reporting whether and how included studies were assessed for quality/risk of bias is therefore a specific expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use standard reporting guidelines for meta-analyses (QUOROM → PRISMA)
rubrics_metrics.description: QUOROM was developed in 1999 to address suboptimal reporting of meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials; PRISMA (2009) updated and broadened that guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopting a standard like QUOROM/PRISMA helps ensure consistent, comprehensive reporting. The original PRISMA statement (2009) and its explanation/elaboration papers provided detailed items to improve reporting of systematic reviews and meta-analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain currency: update guidelines to reflect methodological and terminology advances
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidelines should be updated to incorporate advances in systematic review methodology and terminology occurring since prior versions (motivation for PRISMA 2020).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PRISMA 2020 update process explicitly sought to incorporate methodological and conceptual advances from the prior decade; updates were developed by an international group and documented in methodological papers (e.g., Page et al.). Currency and relevance are criteria for guideline development and revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide explanation and elaboration documents alongside checklists
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting statements should be accompanied by explanation and elaboration papers that clarify items and provide examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The original PRISMA statement was published together with explanation and elaboration papers to help users understand the rationale and implementation of each reporting item. Such companion documents improve usability and adherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic reviews may be required to justify further research
rubrics_metrics.description: Granting agencies may require a systematic review to ensure there is justification for further research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because funders and journals may use systematic reviews to inform decisions about new research or guideline development, reviews should be conducted and reported to a standard that permits their use for these purposes (i.e., comprehensive, transparent, and reproducible).
